findings.paper_title: Treasury Management & Prudential Indicators Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Gross interest earned on investments fell to £545k from £607k despite investment balances quadrupling to £12.4m
findings.detail: Total investments grew from £3.9m to £12.4m (218% increase), but interest earned actually declined by £62k. The council earned 3.90% on investments, marginally below the 3.94% benchmark, reflecting a compressed rate environment that limits the yield benefit of holding larger balances.
findings.matters: As investment rates compress, the same cash balance generates less income, reducing financial flexibility. This constrains the council's ability to fund activities from investment returns and may force reliance on other sources or spending discipline.
findings.figures: Interest earned: £607,187 (2024/25) vs £544,584 (2025/26); investment portfolio £3.9m to £12.4m
findings.quote: Gross interest earned 607,187 544,584

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management & Prudential Indicators Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: The £10m March 2026 borrowing was structured for 5 years because the council is forecasting PWLB longer-term rates to decline within that period
findings.detail: Rather than locking in longer-term borrowing at current elevated rates, the council chose 5-year terms betting on rate falls. The council states: 'The additional loans in 2025/26 were borrowed over 5 years due to the forecast PWLB longer-term rate reducing within 5 years.' This is an explicit interest-rate bet.
findings.matters: If PWLB rates do not fall as forecast and the council must refinance in 5 years at higher rates, it will have foregone the opportunity to lock in current rates. This is a material interest-rate risk for both the lender and council.
findings.figures: £10m borrowed for 5-year terms in March 2026
findings.quote: The additional loans in 2025/26 were borrowed over 5 years due to the forecast PWLB longer-term rate reducing within 5 years.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management & Prudential Indicators Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: HRA financing cost ratio deteriorated to 11.30% (actual) from 10.42% (budgeted), showing worsening debt burden relative to revenue
findings.detail: The ratio of HRA interest costs to net HRA revenue came in at 11.30% actual against a budget of 10.42%—an 88 basis point deterioration. This measure shows the interest cost is consuming a growing share of HRA revenue, driven by £3.066m annual interest payments on debt.
findings.matters: Rising financing cost ratios signal increasing debt burden or shrinking revenue, both red flags for affordability. The HRA's ability to service its self-financing debt is directly tied to this ratio; deterioration limits flexibility and absorbs revenue that could fund service improvements or reserves.
findings.figures: HRA financing costs: 10.42% budgeted, 11.30% actual; annual HRA interest payments £3.066m
findings.quote: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream (note 2)... HRA (applies only to housing authorities) 10.57% 10.42% 11.30%

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management & Prudential Indicators Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Council drew £10m additional PWLB borrowing in March 2026 to fund net unfinanced capital expenditure
findings.detail: In March 2026, the council borrowed £10m from the Public Works Loan Board (£5m HRA, £5m GRA) to cover unfinanced capital spending, raising total borrowing from £88.2m to £98.2m. This was unplanned borrowing beyond the original budget, increasing debt by 11%.
findings.matters: Unplanned mid-year borrowing signals either capital plans changed in-year or available funding fell short. For a lender, this shows the council needing to access capital markets beyond original projections and relying on available headroom within its borrowing limits.
findings.figures: £10m borrowed (£5m HRA, £5m GRA); total borrowing increased to £98.212m
findings.quote: In March 2026 PWLB loans of £10m (£5m HRA and £5m GRA) were drawn by the Council to fund the net unfinanced capital expenditure, leading to a total borrowing at the financial year-end of £98.212m.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management & Prudential Indicators Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: HRA capital programme delivered only 39% of budget: £11.3m actual spend against £29.3m planned
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account capital expenditure came in at £11.3m against a budget of £29.3m—a shortfall of £18m or 62%. While total council capital was £19.4m against £32.9m budgeted, the HRA underspend is material and warrants scrutiny of programme delivery capacity or changing investment priorities in the housing function.
findings.matters: For a lender assessing an HRA-holder, capital delivery is fundamental to the housing business plan and self-financing viability. Large underspends signal either delivery delays, capacity constraints, or changed priorities—all material to risk assessment.
findings.figures: HRA capital: £11.3m actual vs £29.3m budgeted; total capital £19.4m vs £32.9m budgeted
findings.quote: HRA (applies only to housing authorities) 9,419 29,268 11,345

findings.headline: HRA reserves growing to £1.3m (+12%) as outturn favourability masks underlying pressures
findings.detail: The favourable revenue outturn of £357k has been allocated as follows: £226k additional allocation to debt set-aside (to bring total to £3.5m for easier monitoring), and £131k added to HRA balances (bringing them to c. £1.3m). This reserve growth masks the fact that the favourability comes from budget contingency not being used and general cost control, while voids pressures consumed £891k more than forecast.
findings.matters: Growing reserves are healthy, but the composition matters. If reserves are being built by under-spending on essential work (e.g., keeping the contingency unused) rather than by sustainable operations, they mask service delivery risks.
findings.figures: Draft favourable outturn £357k. HRA balances now c. £1.3m (+12% on prior year). Debt set-aside brought to £3.5m. Budget contingency £290k largely unused. Void and repair costs £891k adverse to forecast.
findings.quote: With this amount added, overall HRA balances will be around £1.3m, an increase of around 12%

findings.headline: New £850k per annum commitment for five-year sheltered housing fire door replacement programme
findings.detail: The council has carved out £850k of unused 2025/26 budget to start a multi-year fire door replacement programme on sheltered housing stock. They are seeking approval for £850k per annum for 2027/28–2030/31, creating a £3.4m commitment beyond this year.
findings.matters: This creates a binding multi-year capital commitment (£4.25m total over five years) that wasn't in original planning. It also signals compliance/safety risk: the programme would not exist if doors did not pose a material fire safety hazard.
findings.figures: £850k 2026/27, then £850k per annum for 2027/28 to 2030/31 inclusive (four more years). Total £4.25m.
findings.quote: £850k of unspent 2025/26 budget has been moved to the Sheltered upgrades budget then reprofiled into 2026/27. This is intended to fund the first year of a five year fire door replacement programme on sheltered housing stock.

findings.headline: Capital programme only 53% spent; £2.4m reprofiled, £850k released to reduce borrowing
findings.detail: Of £7.44m revised capital budget, only £3.938m (53%) was spent. £2.414m was reprofiled to 2026/27 for specific schemes (fire safety, smoke detection, re-roofing). A further £850k was released to reduce future borrowing, suggesting original borrowing needs were overstated. Across all capital (including TVD schemes), £11.84m expenditure and £5m funding was reprofiled.
findings.matters: A 47% underspend raises questions about capital project delivery, planning accuracy, and scheme readiness. The decision to release £850k to reduce borrowing indicates the council may have over-borrowed or scheduled projects inaccurately.
findings.figures: Main programme: £7.44m budget, £3.938m spend (53%). General Adaptations 76% spent, Communal Fire Works 33%, Re-roofing 22%, Lifts 96%. Total capital £18.715m budget, £10.796m spend (58%).
findings.quote: The main programme incurred expenditure of £3,938k against revised budget of £7,440k, (53%). It is proposed to reprofile £2,414k of this on specific schemes into 2026/27, the remainder is not required for the scheme it is allocated to, so will be gathered up as a large pot with £850k forming part of the reprofiled amount and the balance released to reduce future borrowing.

findings.headline: £5m external borrowing taken in March 2026; HRA remains under-borrowed by £1.13m
findings.detail: New external borrowing of £5m was drawn in March 2026 for capital purposes. However, the HRA remains £1.13m under-borrowed against its Capital Financing Requirement. The council switched from planned borrowing to capital receipts funding for some schemes. This suggests original capital programme assumptions may not have held.
findings.matters: Under-borrowing can indicate either capital project delays or conservative debt management. The late draw-down of the £5m (March, near year-end) means minimal interest cost this year, but the continuing under-borrowed position suggests capital delivery or funding plans may need reset.
findings.figures: £5m external borrowing March 2026 (interest only £10k as timing late). HRA CFR £94.34m; borrowing £93.21m; under-borrowed £1.13m. April 2025 existing debt £88.21m self-financing.
findings.quote: Although HRA external borrowing was expected it only took place in March 2026 so a favourable timing delay on interest paid.

findings.headline: Voids have become a structural operating problem that management cannot solve
findings.detail: The council has spent two years trying to reduce void levels with additional budget (£300k added for asbestos surveys) and management interventions. Void turnaround times remain elevated despite these efforts: 76 days average in March 2026 against a 55-day target. The council now explicitly states this is 'baked into' the budget, meaning voids are no longer temporary but permanent.
findings.matters: Persistent voids eat into rental income and increase maintenance costs. If management cannot solve this after two years and additional investment, this indicates either systemic property issues, market problems, or operational failures that will continue to drain cash and suppress income.
findings.figures: 380 voids completed in year at average cost of £8,061 per void. Void numbers ranged from 58 to 108 across the year; relet days ranged from 54 to 121 days against 55-day target. £216k council tax pressure from voids.
findings.quote: However, after two years of management action, with additional budget, temporary reductions in void levels and void turnaround then reverting back to higher levels when compared to a few years ago, it seems that higher voids pressure is now baked into the voids service budget and contract.

findings.headline: Ongoing pressures of £993k offset by only £931k of ongoing savings, creating a net ongoing pressure of £62k
findings.detail: The council identified £993k of pressures expected to continue into future years but can only offset £931k through savings, leaving a structural gap of £62k that will carry forward. This is separate from the £3.791m three-year MTFF gap and indicates ongoing structural imbalance between costs and resources.
findings.matters: Even after capturing identified savings, ongoing pressures exceed available ongoing savings, indicating the council cannot sustainably balance future budgets without further action.
findings.figures: £993k ongoing pressures; £931k ongoing savings; £62k net shortfall
findings.quote: It shows that there is around £993k of pressure likely to continue and around £931k of potential savings opportunities.

findings.headline: Car parking income fell £134k short of budget in 2025/26 and the new operating model to correct this remains unimplemented with timing delays
findings.detail: Car parking had a £190k adverse variance in 2025/26, with £134k attributable to income falling below budget. The council is implementing a new car parking model intended to correct this pressure, but timing delays mean the correction may not be fully realised in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Income underperformance in revenue-generating services coupled with delays in implementing a corrective model suggests operational execution risks and raises questions about revenue forecasting reliability.
findings.figures: £190k adverse variance; £134k income shortfall in 2025/26
findings.quote: Car Parking in 2025/26 was £190k adverse compared to budget, around £134k of this relating to income behind budget. Once implemented the new car parking model is expected to correct this pressure. Timing delays mean that this may not be fully realised in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Housing Services faces £357k adverse variance in 2025/26 with £357k of continuing pressures, including £200k from software licences and £157k from NNDR on council assets, plus additional costs when Delf House is mothballed
findings.detail: Housing Services reported an adverse variance of £357k, driven primarily by software licence costs (£200k ongoing pressure) and NNDR on council-owned assets (£157k ongoing). The department expects further pressure in 2026/27 when Delf House is mothballed. Additionally, £129k of grant income available in 2025/26 will not recur in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Housing Services faces mounting structural costs from non-discretionary software spending and property taxes on assets, combined with loss of grant income, indicating sustained pressure in a key service area with limited flexibility to reduce.
findings.figures: £357k adverse variance; £200k software licences (ongoing); £157k NNDR (ongoing); £129k grant income loss (£41k Disabled Facilities + £33k Rough Sleepers + £55k Homelessness Prevention)
findings.quote: Housing Services adverse variance of £358k is primarily due to £200k of likely ongoing pressure from software licences that are not being capitalised, plus £157k of ongoing pressure from NNDR on WLBC GRA assets, particularly for the main Council office sites. In 2026/27 there is likely to be further additional pressure when Delf House is mothballed.

findings.headline: Environmental Services has £192k of unbudgeted fleet lease pressure emerging in 2027/28 due to contract renegotiation being missed from the budget cycle
findings.detail: The five-year fleet lease contract was renegotiated in 2025/26 but the resulting cost impact was not captured in the 2026/27 budget-setting process, creating an unbudgeted pressure for 2027/28. This comes on top of £162k adverse variance in 2025/26 from fleet and agency costs.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted pressures emerging from routine contract renegotiation suggest gaps in the council's budget planning and cost tracking processes, and indicate further forward-year budget pressures.
findings.figures: £192k additional unbudgeted lease contract pressure in 2027/28; £162k adverse variance in 2025/26
findings.quote: The five year fleet lease contract was renegotiated in 2025/26 but missed the 2026/27 budget setting cycle so there is an additional unbudgeted lease contract pressure in 2027/28 of around £192k.

findings.headline: The council faces a £3.791m funding gap across three years to March 2029
findings.detail: The February 2026 MTFF identified a continuing medium-term gap of £3.791m for the three-year period to March 2029. This represents a structural funding shortfall that the council will need to address through further savings, income generation, or borrowing.
findings.matters: A multi-year funding gap of this scale indicates the council faces sustained structural budget pressures beyond the current year, affecting financial sustainability and future borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £3.791m gap for three years to March 2029; earlier MTFF (March 2025) showed £1.315m gap for 2026/27 and £0.687m for 2027/28
findings.quote: The MTFF approved in February 2026 showed an improved position for 2026/27 but a continuing medium-term gap of £3.791m for the three years to March 2029.

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation transition costs budgeted at £0.4m but explicitly flagged as likely to increase materially
findings.detail: The capital programme includes £0.400m for the 'LGR Transition & Transformation Scheme', but the council states this 'will be reviewed as information is received and may need to be increased further.' This is an unquantified cost risk that will impact capital budgets as the reorganisation process develops.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand unquantified financial commitments. If LGR transition costs increase significantly, this will directly reduce capital funding available for other schemes or require increased borrowing, affecting the council's medium-term financial position.
findings.figures: £0.400m currently allocated for LGR Transition & Transformation; future increase amount unquantified
findings.quote: The LGR Transition & Transformation Scheme will be reviewed as information is received and may need to be increased further

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered only 48% of approved budget, with £8.7m unspent due to LGR planning disruption
findings.detail: Actual capital expenditure was £8.086m against an approved budget of £16.812m, leaving £8.725m unspent (52% of budget). The council explicitly states the capital programme was 'reviewed by officers to determine the best use of resources going forward' considering local government reorganisation, indicating strategic uncertainty is constraining deployment.
findings.matters: A 52% underspend raises questions about the council's forecasting accuracy and capital delivery capability. The explicit link to LGR review suggests major schemes are being held pending reorganisation outcomes, creating uncertainty for medium-term planning.
findings.figures: £8.086m expenditure, £16.812m budget, £8.725m underspend
findings.quote: Expenditure on the GRA Capital Programme in the year was £8.086m against a budget of £16.812m, an underspend of £8.725m

findings.headline: Accommodation strategy deferred indefinitely, removing major capital commitment from plan
findings.detail: A previously approved capital scheme for accommodation strategy is now on hold. The paper indicates this project is in the capital programme budgets but provides no clarity on timing or expected cost, leaving the future of this investment uncertain.
findings.matters: A major capital project has been deferred, suggesting either affordability concerns or strategic paralysis pending local government reorganisation outcomes. Both signals matter to lenders assessing the council's financial management and delivery capability.
findings.figures: Amount not disclosed in paper
findings.quote: the accommodation strategy however this project is on hold

findings.headline: The council's 2024-25 accounts received a disclaimed audit opinion, as did 2021-22 and 2022-23, resulting in three years without clean audit opinions.
findings.detail: The 2024-25 audit resulted in a disclaimed opinion with no explanation provided. The 2021-22 and 2022-23 accounts also received disclaimed opinions on 13 December 2024 because Grant Thornton determined there was insufficient time to effectively audit them. Disclaimed opinions mean the auditor cannot provide assurance on the accounts.
findings.matters: Multiple years without clean audit opinions reduce transparency on the council's financial position and indicate material gaps in audit assurance; this is a governance concern for lenders assessing council creditworthiness.
findings.quote: The 2024/25 audit of the accounts resulted in a disclaimed opinion and no new audit recommendation were issued.

findings.headline: The external auditor identified the need to continue building capacity and resilience in the Finance Team, work that remains in progress.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's Value for Money assessment recommended the council 'Continue to build capacity and resilience into the Finance Team', indicating the audit found the finance function has capacity constraints. This work is still in progress.
findings.matters: Finance team capacity constraints increase risk of poor controls, errors, delayed reporting, and difficulty managing financial challenges; auditor concerns about current capacity suggest vulnerabilities in financial management.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Continue to build capacity and resilience into the Finance Team (In progress).

findings.headline: The council had to address a gap in the Medium Term Financial Strategy and reduce reliance on reserves, now marked complete.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's Value for Money assessment identified that West Lancashire had a gap in its MTFS and was relying on reserves. The council has now completed actions to address this, though the recommendation will remain open until formally confirmed in the 2025-26 audit.
findings.matters: An MTFS gap indicates the council's budget was not balanced through recurring revenues; reliance on reserves to bridge gaps suggests using one-off funding for recurring costs, which is unsustainable and a core concern for lenders.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: To address the gap in the MTFS and reduce reliance on reserves (Complete).

findings.headline: Leisure centre provision creates a residual financial pressure that remains unresolved in the Medium Term Financial Strategy.
findings.detail: The financial impact of the Council's leisure centres has been factored into the MTFS. Savings proposals have been agreed to help mitigate this impact, but a residual financial pressure remains over the medium-term planning period.
findings.matters: Leisure centres represent an ongoing deficit requiring Council subsidy. This reduces financial flexibility and may force cuts to other services.
findings.figures: Residual financial pressure remaining over MTFS period; amounts not disclosed in this document
findings.quote: A residual financial pressure remains over the period of the MTFS.

findings.headline: The Council has an unresolved budget gap in its Medium Term Financial Strategy despite agreeing some savings proposals.
findings.detail: The MTFS identified an ongoing budget gap and financial pressures. While savings proposals have been agreed by Council, further decisions are required and a budget gap remains unresolved over the medium term. The Council needs to identify and deliver additional savings.
findings.matters: An unresolved budget gap forces difficult spending decisions and may require service reductions or reserves drawdown. Lenders assess this as financial sustainability risk.
findings.figures: Budget gap identified and ongoing; specific quantum not disclosed in this document
findings.quote: A budget gap remains over the medium term, and further work is required to identify and deliver additional savings.

findings.headline: Internal Audit was not maintained at statutory levels during 2025/26 due to staff departures, leaving a period with no effective independent assurance.
findings.detail: The Council's in-house audit team experienced significant resource constraints following staff departures. Delivery of the approved audit plan was materially affected and there was no effective Internal Audit provision for part of the year. A new external provider was appointed and came into place from April 2026.
findings.matters: Internal Audit is a fundamental control mechanism. Its absence means weaknesses in financial management, compliance, and risk may go undetected. Lenders rely on audit assurance as evidence of organisational control.
findings.figures: One audit provider transition during the year; new provider appointed April 2026
findings.quote: Delivery of the approved audit plan in 2025/26 was materially affected by sustained resourcing constraints following staff departures. There was no effective Internal Audit provision for part of the year.

findings.headline: Procurement compliance issues unresolved despite claims of imminent completion; follow-up audit added
findings.detail: Although procurement compliance recommendations are stated to be 'due to be completed in the next few weeks', the council has added a follow-up audit in 2026/27, signalling underlying concern about the timeliness or quality of remediation.
findings.matters: Procurement control failures can result in overspending, fraud, or failure to achieve value for money. The decision to add a follow-up audit suggests the council itself is uncertain about the remediation.
findings.figures: Not quantified; but significant enough to warrant dedicated follow-up audit
findings.quote: Given the significance of Procurement Compliance, even though all recommendations are due to be completed in the next few weeks, a follow up audit will also be added to the 2026/27 audit plan

findings.headline: Staff turnover in finance and audit functions has delayed implementation of audit recommendations for years
findings.detail: The council identifies staff turnover as the primary reason recommendations have remained outstanding 'over the last few years', with loss of knowledge about original audit findings and remediation requirements.
findings.matters: High turnover in audit and finance roles suggests capacity or retention problems that could affect financial control, compliance, and reporting quality.
findings.figures: Not quantified; affects recommendations dating to 2021/22 (4+ years old)
findings.quote: Over the last few years a number of recommendations have remained outstanding mainly due to staff turnover and therefore a lack of knowledge regarding the original practice and the recommendations made.

findings.headline: 21 grant management control recommendations unresolved, deferred to external audit plan
findings.detail: A significant backlog of unresolved grant management audit findings has been handed to external audit rather than resolved internally, indicating ongoing control weaknesses over grant administration.
findings.matters: Grant mismanagement or control failures could result in grant clawback, funding penalties, or unaccounted public money, directly affecting council finances.
findings.figures: 21 outstanding recommendations in grant management
findings.quote: Grant Management (21 outstanding recommendations)

findings.headline: 10 business continuity audit recommendations remain unresolved and are deferred to 2026/27 audit plan
findings.detail: Business continuity weaknesses identified in past audits have not been remediated and are now being carried forward as part of the forward audit plan for Veritau Ltd, the council's external audit provider.
findings.matters: Business continuity failures could disrupt a council's ability to operate and deliver services, directly affecting its ability to manage finances and repay borrowing.
findings.figures: 10 outstanding recommendations in business continuity
findings.quote: Business Continuity (10 outstanding recommendations)

findings.headline: 29 critical-priority audit findings remain unresolved after a 5-year backlog
findings.detail: As of 1 April 2026, there are 29 critical and 55 high priority recommendations outstanding from audits dating back to 2021/22. Only 67 (38%) of the 177 open recommendations have been closed; 45% are still in progress with no guaranteed completion date for the remainder.
findings.matters: A lender assessing financial stability needs to understand the control environment. Unresolved critical audit findings spanning years indicate control weaknesses or inability to implement remediation.
findings.figures: 29 critical (16% of total), 55 high priority (31%), 177 total open recommendations
findings.quote: At the end of March 2026 there were 177 open recommendations covering a 5 year period of which 175 are outstanding.

findings.headline: Treasury investment balances projected to collapse to £0.15m by 2027-28, reducing liquidity buffer
findings.detail: Expected investment balances are forecast to decline 98% from £7.3m in 2024-25 to £0.15m in 2027-28, then recover only to £1.2m in 2028-29. Fund balances are also declining from £12.9m to £10.8m. This represents a material reduction in the council's liquid cash reserves and working capital cushion.
findings.matters: A lender would view depletion of liquid reserves as a credit negative. Near-zero investment balances eliminate the council's buffer for managing unexpected cash flows or contingencies, increasing dependence on credit facilities and reducing financial flexibility.
findings.quote: Expected investments 7.300 1.973 1.827 0.152 1.230

findings.headline: Council external debt projected to rise from £88.2m to £202.5m over four years (increase of £114.3m)
findings.detail: External debt is forecast to increase dramatically, with the majority (£86.7m) being HRA debt rising from £88.2m to £174.9m. The borrowing requirement peaks at £42.4m in 2026-27 (the fiscal year covered by this strategy). This debt trajectory is policy-driven and necessary to fund the capital programmes, but represents material leverage relative to council size and revenue.
findings.matters: A lender would assess debt levels as a key credit metric. The projected increase in leverage, concentrated in HRA, creates questions about debt service capacity and sustainability if income or reserves fail to support repayment.

findings.headline: HRA capital expenditure programme surges to £50.5m in 2026-27, more than doubling from prior years
findings.detail: HRA capital spending is forecast to increase from £23.6m in 2025-26 to £50.5m in 2026-27, representing a major step-change from historical levels of around £9-10m. The programme then moderates to £34-42m in subsequent years. This concentrates heavy capital investment into the housing stock during 2026-27.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand the purpose and business case for this major capital programme, expected returns, and whether rental income can adequately support the resulting debt obligations.
findings.figures: HRA capital expenditure: 2024-25 actual £9.4m, 2025-26 estimate £23.6m, 2026-27 estimate £50.5m, 2027-28 £33.8m, 2028-29 £41.9m

findings.headline: £3.7m capital expenditure slippage from 2025/26 into 2026/27 due to implementation delays
findings.detail: Schemes across Environmental Services and Wellbeing and Place services have experienced delays, with £3.711m of expenditure now rephased from the current year into 2026/27. This indicates delivery challenges in programme implementation.
findings.matters: Slippage in scheme delivery can indicate project management challenges or external barriers to execution, and may foreshadow further delays in the expanding 2026/27 programme.
findings.figures: £3.711m slippage
findings.quote: £3.711m has been identified as slippage, being expenditure originally expected to be incurred in 2025/26 but now rephased into the 2026/27 programme. This is mainly due to delays in implementation of a number of schemes across Environmental Services and Wellbeing and Place

findings.headline: Skelmersdale Town Centre Masterplan approved but unfunded and unscheduled; no commencement date or figures included in capital programme
findings.detail: The council approved the Skelmersdale Town Centre Masterplan at Council in April 2025, but commencement dates remain unconfirmed and the scheme is explicitly excluded from this capital strategy with no financial figures or timeline.
findings.matters: A major approved project without identified funding or schedule represents a latent capital demand that could emerge during or beyond the strategy period and require new financing.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Skelmersdale Town Centre Masterplan was approved at Council in April 2025. Commencement dates for this scheme have not been finalised yet and figures have therefore not been included within the strategy report at this time.

findings.headline: LGR transformation costs have contingency: £600k allocated but early indications suggest a further £400k may be needed
findings.detail: The council has allocated £600k for Local Government Reorganisation transition and transformation costs. However, preliminary discussions with Lancashire County Council and other authorities indicate early indications are that a further £400k may be required. This represents an unquantified contingent cost.
findings.matters: Reorganisation transition costs could exceed budget by up to 67%, creating unexpected demands on capital resources or cash during a critical transition period.
findings.figures: £600k allocated, further £400k potentially required
findings.quote: Following Preliminary discussions with Lancashire County Council and other Local Authorities within Lancashire early indications are that a further £400k may be required for LGR transformation.

findings.headline: Revenue budget impact of £94m borrowing increase acknowledged but not yet fully quantified
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that increased capital borrowing will increase revenue costs through interest charges and minimum revenue provision, but states the full impact will emerge only when assets are finalised. The council forecasts MRP of £0.5m in 2026/27, £0.9m in 2027/28, and £0.9m in 2028/29, but does not show how interest costs will be met.
findings.matters: If the full revenue impact of £94m additional borrowing is not yet calculated or included in revenue projections, it represents a latent budget risk. The council may face unplanned revenue pressures.
findings.quote: Additionally, this will have an impact on revenue with increased interest charges and minimum revenue provision once the assets are finalised.

findings.headline: HRA thermal/ventilation/drainage expenditure surges to £28.2m in 2026/27, nearly five times the current year
findings.detail: The HRA capital programme shows TVD expenditure jumping from £5.520m in 2025/26 to £28.244m in 2026/27, remaining elevated at £20.440m in 2027/28 and £31.670m in 2028/29. This represents a sustained and substantial increase in HRA capital needs, primarily financed through borrowing (£32.721m HRA borrowing in 2026/27).
findings.matters: A major surge in essential capital works indicates either previously under-resourced asset maintenance or new compliance/decarbonisation obligations. Either way, it represents a sustained material increase in HRA capital and borrowing needs.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increases by £94m over three years, driven by substantial new borrowing
findings.detail: The council plans to increase borrowing significantly, with £9.649m prudential borrowing in the General Fund in 2026/27 alone, and £32.721m in the HRA. The total increase in CFR over three years is £94m, which will drive up both interest costs and minimum revenue provision. The council explicitly flags that consideration must be given to the affordability of this borrowing increase.
findings.matters: A £94m increase in borrowing requirement over three years represents a substantial change in the council's debt trajectory and will materially increase revenue costs. A lender needs to assess whether the council can service this debt.
findings.figures: £94.0m CFR increase, £9.649m GRA prudential borrowing 2026/27, £32.721m HRA borrowing 2026/27
findings.quote: The increase in budget on both GRA and HRA capital programmes will lead to an increase in the Capital Financing Requirement of £94.0m over the next 3 years and thus an increase in borrowing for the Council.

findings.headline: Reserve drawdowns of £605k used to support the 2026/27 revenue budget; transformation reserve halved from £1.1m to £500k.
findings.detail: The council is releasing £605k from reserves (including £30k general slippage reserve and £575k from other reserves) plus £87k heating reserve to support 2026/27 revenue. The Transformation & Efficiency Savings Reserve is being reduced from £1.1m to £500k. This provides medium-term flexibility but indicates tightness in the revenue budget.
findings.matters: Drawdown of reserves to fund revenue budgets suggests the operating budget is tight. If reserves are used, they are no longer available as a cushion for unexpected pressures. A lender monitors reserve adequacy relative to volatility.
findings.figures: £605k reserve releases in 2026/27; Transformation reserve reduced from £1,100k to £500k; overall HRA reserves £2.75m (8.3% of total revenue budget)
findings.quote: £600k from HRA Transformation & Efficiency Savings revenue reserve... £30k from slippage reserve... £87k from heating reserve

findings.headline: Major capital programme: £40.5m planned in 2026/27 (£22.2m housing investment + £18.2m new build), largest spending in the business plan.
findings.detail: The HRA capital programme in 2026/27 is substantial, including £22.245m on kitchens, bathrooms, electrics, heating, roofs, and other housing stock works, plus £18.244m on new build homes through TVDL. This level of spending will require the new external borrowing and places significant pressure on the council's capital financing and cash management.
findings.matters: Lenders assess whether capital spending is sustainable and properly funded. Large capital programmes that depend on external borrowing increase debt service costs and must be matched against revenue capability.
findings.figures: Total capital expenditure 2026/27: £40.489m (including £22.245m housing investment, £18.244m new build TVDL); funded by grants £6.945m, capital receipts £2.716m, revenue contribution £3.489m, borrowing £22.721m
findings.quote: Total Capital Expenditure [2026/27]: 40,489 [£000]... Borrowing -22,721 [£000]

findings.headline: Ten-year government rent settlement (CPI+1%) announced, replacing five-year settlement; significant uplift to HRA cash flow outlook.
findings.detail: Government has extended the rent policy from five to ten years of CPI+1% annual increases. The paper notes this has had a significant favourable impact on the 30-year business plan. The 2026/27 budget assumes 4.8% rent increases (CPI 3.8% + 1%), in line with this policy.
findings.matters: A lender assesses a council's revenue predictability. A ten-year rent settlement provides certainty for both rents and therefore service coverage ratios. This improves the council's creditworthiness and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: CPI+1% settlement extended to 10 years; 4.8% rent increase in 2026/27; dwelling rents forecast -£29.650m (revenue)
findings.quote: During 2025/26 Government announced that the current rent settlement of annual increases in rents of CPI + 1% will be increased from five to ten years. This has had a significant favourable impact on the HRA business plan in the medium- and long-term.

findings.headline: Self-financing debt repayment set-aside ending; £4.4m tranche due March 2027 to be reborrowed, not repaid.
findings.detail: For 15 years, the council set aside £416k annually to cushion repayment of self-financing borrowing tranches. From 2026/27, this practice ends. The £4.4m first tranche due March 2027 will be reborrowed rather than repaid. This is justified by relaxed HRA borrowing rules and the more generous 10-year rent settlement.
findings.matters: The council is changing debt management strategy: instead of reducing debt, it is refinancing it. This extends debt maturity and increases total debt service costs over time, affecting long-term affordability.
findings.figures: £416k annual set-aside ceases; £4.4m tranche due March 2027 to be reborrowed
findings.quote: Given the relaxation of HRA borrowing rules, the reality that self-financing debt in March 2027 is likely to be externally reborrowed over the medium term and the more generous rent settlement, self-financing set aside will be ceased as a matter of course from 2026/27. The first tranche of £4.4m is due for repayment in March 2027 so the direct impact of this will be in 2027/28 as it is likely that the £4.4m will be reborrowed then.

findings.headline: First external borrowing in many years, starting Q4 2025/26, to fund capital works.
findings.detail: The council has been free from external borrowing for many years beyond the 2012 self-financing debt. Changing economic conditions and ambitious capital plans now make external borrowing necessary. HRA borrowing of up to £4.725m is assumed in Q4 2025/26, with further borrowing likely in 2026/27 to fund the large capital programme.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's new debt position, covenant headroom, and the sustainability of increased debt service as capital spending increases.
findings.figures: £4.725m external HRA borrowing assumed Q4 2025/26; £200k interest budgeted on this in 2026/27; further £200k assumed for additional 2026/27 borrowing
findings.quote: The changing economic environment and ambitious capital plans within both the GRA and the HRA mean it is likely that WLBC external borrowing will be required in Q4 of 2025/26. For HRA budget setting purposes it has been assumed that external HRA borrowing in 2025/26 will be up to £4.725m

findings.paper_title: GRA Revenue Budget Report and MTFS Update 26-29 Council v2
findings.headline: Positive: Pension fund now in surplus; contribution rate reduced 7.4 percentage points saving £1.189m
findings.detail: The 2023 triennial valuation showed the pension fund has moved into surplus, reducing employer contribution rates from 16.7% to 9.3%, delivering £1.189m saving. A further decision expected end January 2026 on contingency levels may yield additional gains.
findings.matters: Pension deficits are a long-term liability risk for councils. This valuation result materially reduces the council's structural cost base and long-term liability exposure.
findings.figures: £1.189m saving; contribution rate reduced from 16.7% to 9.3%
findings.quote: Reduction in employers' pension contributions from 16.7% to 9.3% as a result of the triennial valuation demonstrating an increase in the surplus on the pension fund. A decision is expected at the end of January 2026 on the contingency level which may deliver further benefits.

findings.paper_title: GRA Revenue Budget Report and MTFS Update 26-29 Council v2
findings.headline: Business rates baseline reset delivers transitional protection in 2026/27 but creates £0.180m pressure in 2027/28
findings.detail: Government overestimated rates growth for pooling authorities, reducing support grant by £0.432m in 2026/27. While compensated by adjustment in that year, the protection ends and creates a £0.180m embedded pressure in 2027/28 with funding levels unchanged thereafter.
findings.matters: Baseline reset creates structural income uncertainty. Transitional protections are temporary, and the council must absorb future reductions through spending cuts.
findings.figures: £0.432m reduction (compensated in 2026/27); £0.180m pressure in 2027/28
findings.quote: The government had overestimated the growth in rates for authorities in pooling arrangements in the provisional settlement meaning a reduction of £0.432m of Revenue Support Funding for 2026-27. However, to ensure local authorities do not lose out an adjustment to the support grant of £0.432m has been applied so there is no impact in 2026-27. There is a reduction in 2027-28 resulting in a pressure of £0.180m

findings.paper_title: GRA Revenue Budget Report and MTFS Update 26-29 Council v2
findings.headline: Property income loss: Co-operative Bank vacating Delf House creates £0.336m annual income shortfall
findings.detail: The Co-operative Bank has given notice to vacate Delf House in June 2026, resulting in loss of rental income of £0.336m now embedded as a permanent pressure in 2026/27 budget onwards.
findings.matters: Asset income loss signals either reduced strategic tenancy value or failed property strategy. This income is now permanently lost from the budget.
findings.figures: £0.336m loss of income
findings.quote: £0.336m which relates to the loss of income at Delf House now the Co-operative Bank have given notice to vacate the site in June 2026

findings.paper_title: GRA Revenue Budget Report and MTFS Update 26-29 Council v2
findings.headline: Food waste collection introduces £0.602m recurring, unfunded cost pressure from 2027/28
findings.detail: Introduction of food waste collections will create an ongoing budget pressure of £0.602m in 2027/28 and £0.015m in 2028/29. While existing EPR and Food Waste grant funding covers the cost in 2026/27, the recurring operational cost from 2027/28 onwards is embedded in the forecast deficit and unfunded.
findings.matters: This is a structural, permanent cost increase from new legislation that cannot be reversed or reduced. It represents service growth funded from a shrinking budget base.
findings.quote: an ongoing budget pressure of £0.602m in 2027/28 and a further £0.015m in 2028/29 has been incorporated into the MTFF

findings.paper_title: GRA Revenue Budget Report and MTFS Update 26-29 Council v2
findings.headline: Structural pattern of annual reserve depletion: £1.962m drawn 2023/24, £1.655m drawn 2024/25
findings.detail: The council drew £1.962m from reserves in 2023-24 and £1.655m in 2024-25, with £0.865m budgeted for 2025/26 (though Q2 forecast suggests it may balance). The S151 officer explicitly warns: 'Continued use of reserves is clearly unsustainable.' This pattern indicates structural, not cyclical, deficits.
findings.matters: Repeated annual deficits despite ongoing savings proposals signal the council is spending significantly above its sustainable income base and cannot be managed through one-off measures.
findings.quote: 2023-24 required £1.962m of reserves and 2024-25 required reserves of £1.655m to address in year overspends. Continued use of reserves is clearly unsustainable.

findings.paper_title: GRA Revenue Budget Report and MTFS Update 26-29 Council v2
findings.headline: Budget gap of £3.791m across 2027/28–2028/29 against available reserves of only £1.993m
findings.detail: The council faces a cumulative budget deficit of £2.540m in 2027/28 and £1.251m in 2028/29. Available reserves (excluding earmarked and ring-fenced reserves) are forecast at only £1.993m by end of 2025/26. The S151 officer notes that without ability to fund this gap from reserves, the council would require application for Exceptional Financial Support or be forced to issue a Section 114 notice.
findings.matters: A lender must assess whether a council has sufficient reserves to absorb forecasted deficits. A gap this large relative to reserves signals insolvency risk and potential statutory intervention.
findings.figures: £3.791m total gap (£2.540m 2027/28; £1.251m 2028/29); £1.993m available reserves
findings.quote: a significant gap of £3.791m across the medium-term against total usable reserves of £1.993m is currently forecast

findings.headline: Accommodation Strategy capital project removed from 2026/27-2028/29 capital programme
findings.detail: A new capital project titled 'Accommodation Strategy' has been removed from the capital programme, releasing £1.5m of capital receipts. The capital receipts are being reallocated to smaller schemes and to reduce prudential borrowing, rather than funding this strategy.
findings.matters: Removal of a named capital strategy project indicates either deprioritization or financial constraints. A lender would want to understand why a planned accommodation initiative did not proceed.
findings.figures: £1.5 million of capital receipts released
findings.quote: That the new capital project 'the Accommodation Strategy' be removed. That the £1.5million of capital receipts, released as a result of the non-inclusion of the Accommodation Strategy in the capital programme, be reallocated

findings.headline: Chapel Gallery Ormskirk essential re-roofing works under-funded, requiring additional £200,000 allocation
findings.detail: The council is adding £200k in 2026/27 specifically because the current capital allocation for Chapel Gallery Ormskirk is described as inadequate to cover necessary re-roofing and other essential works. This signals a gap in original capital planning for essential asset maintenance.
findings.matters: A lender assessing council finances needs to know whether essential asset maintenance is properly budgeted and whether the council can maintain its property portfolio without unplanned reallocations.
findings.quote: An additional £200,000 in 2026/27 to the existing capital budget to allow for the re-roofing and other essential works at Chapel Gallery Ormskirk, as the current allocation is inadequate

findings.paper_title: 6. WLBC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 - FINAL FOR COMMITTEE
findings.headline: Internal audit gave a minimal assurance rating on procurement compliance with 15 recommendations open
findings.detail: Despite updates to Contract Procedure Rules and alignment to the Procurement Act 2023, the council has compliance weaknesses including missing documentation and non-adherence to procedures. 15 open recommendations remain at the time of reporting.
findings.matters: Procurement control weaknesses can result in overpaying suppliers or legal challenges to contracts, further pressuring budgets.
findings.figures: 15 open recommendations; minimal assurance rating
findings.quote: Despite updated Contract Procedure Rules and a new strategy aligned to the Procurement Act 2023, compliance weaknesses persist. Internal Audit issued a Minimal Assurance rating, citing missing documentation and non-adherence to procedures. 15 recommendations remain open as at the time of reporting.

findings.paper_title: 6. WLBC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 - FINAL FOR COMMITTEE
findings.headline: A 2022/23 governance recommendation to present the Corporate Risk Register as a standalone item remains unaddressed after three years
findings.detail: The auditor flagged that risks remain misaligned with strategic objectives and the risk register is not presented separately to the Audit & Governance Committee. This outstanding recommendation from 2022/23 signals slow governance implementation.
findings.matters: Long-standing unaddressed governance gaps indicate weak capacity or willingness to implement audit recommendations, raising questions about broader governance effectiveness.
findings.figures: Recommendation outstanding since 2022/23
findings.quote: However, the Corporate Risk Register was not presented as a standalone item, and risks remain misaligned with strategic objectives—a recommendation from 2022/23 still outstanding.

findings.paper_title: 6. WLBC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 - FINAL FOR COMMITTEE
findings.headline: Root causes of overspend include persistent rises in leisure costs, agency staffing and income shortfalls that budgets do not account for
findings.detail: The council's budgets are being exceeded by rising costs in leisure services, agency staffing, and fleet maintenance, alongside reduced income from leisure centres, planning, building control, car parking and markets. The council notes it only provides inflation in contracts, not general price inflation, creating potential overoptimism.
findings.matters: These are structural service cost and income pressures that cannot be addressed by one-off freezes, indicating the budget baseline is unsustainable.
findings.figures: Affects leisure, staffing, fleet, and income-generating services
findings.quote: Officers clearly articulate the cause of the underling financial pressures in their financial reporting to Members, which are pervasive across a range of services. These include rising costs in leisure services, agency staffing, fleet damage and repairs, compounded by reductions in income from leisure centres, planning, building control, car parking and markets.

findings.paper_title: 6. WLBC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 - FINAL FOR COMMITTEE
findings.headline: Council is forecasting an emerging £594k in-year overspend in 2025/26 at quarter one
findings.detail: Continuing the pattern of in-year overspends, the council's Q1 position shows it is tracking to underspend its budget by £594k. If unaddressed, this represents another unplanned call on reserves.
findings.matters: The pattern of consistent overspends despite recruitment freezes and spending controls indicates budgeting assumptions are optimistic or service demand is structurally unmanageable.
findings.figures: £594k Q1 2025/26 forecast shortfall
findings.quote: A similar trajectory is emerging in 2025/26, at Q1 position the Council is forecasting a £594k shortfall against budget by year end, which if unaddressed in year would be an additional unplanned call on reserves.

findings.paper_title: 6. WLBC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 - FINAL FOR COMMITTEE
findings.headline: The council could not agree enough savings to close the 2025/26 budget gap and required reserves instead
findings.detail: Members initially rejected the proposed savings package, particularly closure of leisure facilities. A revised package of £0.895m in savings was eventually approved in March 2025, but this left £0.865m of the £1.76m underlying gap to be closed by using reserves.
findings.matters: Inability to agree and deliver savings indicates the council lacks the political will or management capacity to address structural deficits, meaning budget pressures will recur.
findings.figures: £1.76m budget gap identified; £0.895m savings approved; £0.865m closed via reserves
findings.quote: At this stage the budget was not agreed by Members, who did not approve all proposed savings schemes, specifically in relation to leisure facility closures. As a result a £1.76m budget gap for 2025/26 remained. The budget was finally approved in March where £895k of replacement savings were approved, therefore leaving £865k to be met from reserves to produce a balanced budget.

findings.paper_title: 6. WLBC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 - FINAL FOR COMMITTEE
findings.headline: Auditor identifies significant weakness in financial sustainability arrangements, continued from prior year
findings.detail: The auditor flagged this weakness last year and it persists. Officers have articulated that continued reserve usage is unsustainable, yet the council has continued to make decisions that rely on reserves in both the short and medium-term.
findings.matters: A continuing significant audit weakness directly signals credit risk and may trigger covenant scrutiny from existing lenders.
findings.figures: Weakness identified in 2023/24 and continues in 2024/25
findings.quote: In the prior year we identified a weakness in the Council's arrangements to secure medium-term financial sustainability as a result of its savings and reserves arrangements. Some progress has been observed in relation to savings. However, although officers set out the implications of reserve usage as being unsustainable, decisions have continued to be made to rely on reserves in the short and medium-term.

findings.paper_title: 6. WLBC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 - FINAL FOR COMMITTEE
findings.headline: Reserves projected to fall to dangerously low levels unless structural budget gaps are closed
findings.detail: The council used £1.1m of budgeted reserves in 2024/25, then overspent by a further £0.7m. For 2025/26, £0.865m of reserves are budgeted against an underlying £1.76m gap. A medium-term gap of £2m extends to 2027/28, and an emerging Q1 shortfall of £594k suggests further in-year pressure. Unallocated reserves at start of 2025/26 are £2.92m.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves leave the council unable to respond to unexpected costs, service disruptions, or changes in funding, directly affecting its creditworthiness and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £1.1m budgeted 2024/25 + £0.7m overspend; £0.865m budgeted 2025/26; £2m medium-term gap; £594k Q1 2025/26 shortfall; £2.92m opening reserves
findings.quote: Should alternative solutions not be found to these gaps there would be an additional call on reserves, reducing them to dangerously low levels and vulnerable to further emerging overspends.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for INTERNAL AUDIT ANNUAL REPORT AND OPINION 2024/25
findings.headline: Fraud risk assessment identifies resource gaps in prevention and detection
findings.detail: CIPFA's fraud and corruption self-assessment produced an action plan identifying areas where resources are required to ensure adequate arrangements for fraud prevention and detection. The council received 3,178 possible fraud matches from the National Fraud Initiative to investigate.
findings.matters: Unresourced fraud controls and a backlog of NFI matches represent a gap in detection capability that could allow material fraud to go undetected.
findings.figures: 3,178 NFI possible matches received; fraud action plan identifies resource requirements
findings.quote: The CCGM completed the CIPFA Managing the Risk of Fraud and Corruption self-assessment during the year and produced an action plan that has been shared with EMT. The action plan details several areas where resources are required to ensure that there are adequate arrangements in place for the prevention and detection of fraud... the Council has received 3178 possible matches.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for INTERNAL AUDIT ANNUAL REPORT AND OPINION 2024/25
findings.headline: Internal control framework opinion downgraded to Limited (second-worst rating)
findings.detail: The CCGM opinion on the council's internal control environment is Limited, not Moderate. This rating reflects slow progress implementing previous audit recommendations, delay in the payroll system implementation, staffing resource issues in the governance service, and the Limited and Minimal assurance audit reports.
findings.matters: A Limited (not Substantial or Moderate) internal control opinion means medium risk that objectives may not be achieved and there is scope for material error or loss.
findings.figures: 1 Limited internal control opinion out of 3 framework areas assessed (Governance: Moderate; Risk Management: Moderate; Internal Control: Limited)
findings.quote: Having considered the findings from the programme of Internal Audit reviews undertaken during the year, it is clear to see that there has been a marked improvement in the number of audit reviews with a substantial or moderate assurances rating. However, the CCGM has balanced these improvements with the slow progress made in implementing recommendations from previous years, the delay in the implementation of the new payroll system, staffing resource issues within Corporate Compliance and Governance Service and the Limited and No Assurance reports. The opinion in relation to this area is Limited.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for INTERNAL AUDIT ANNUAL REPORT AND OPINION 2024/25
findings.headline: Infrastructure compliance failures in electricity and gas safety
findings.detail: Both electric and gas compliance audits received Limited Assurance opinions (medium risk), indicating controls are poorly designed or inconsistently applied. The audit notes these are issues that require immediate management attention and could mean objectives are not achieved.
findings.matters: Safety and statutory compliance failures on building infrastructure create operational, reputational and liability risk for the council.
findings.figures: 2 out of 21 audits rated Limited Assurance for infrastructure compliance
findings.quote: Electric – Compliance Limited; Gas – Compliance Limited

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for INTERNAL AUDIT ANNUAL REPORT AND OPINION 2024/25
findings.headline: Large backlog of unimplemented audit recommendations with external auditor criticism
findings.detail: The council has a high number of outstanding audit recommendations from 2021/22 onwards. The External Auditor has commented on this issue. The Deputy Chief Executive has explicitly instructed Corporate Management Team members to address outstanding and overdue recommendations without delay, and the Internal Audit Service are still reviewing evidence of implementation.
findings.matters: A large backlog of unresolved audit findings indicates controls are not being fixed, and lender concerns about audit discipline and management follow-through are material.
findings.figures: Outstanding from 2021/22 onwards; described as 'high number' and 'numbers remain high'
findings.quote: There remains a high number of outstanding audit recommendations from 2021/22 onwards... Whilst there has been a reduction in outstanding audit recommendations from previous years, numbers remain high and the Council's External Auditor has commented on this in their Annual Report. The Deputy Chief Executive has explicitly instructed CMT members to address the outstanding and overdue recommendations without delay.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for INTERNAL AUDIT ANNUAL REPORT AND OPINION 2024/25
findings.headline: Staffing collapse in governance, risk and compliance function with no replacement plan
findings.detail: Four key officers leaving: the Corporate Compliance and Governance Manager, Risk Management and Insurance Officer, Information Governance Manager and Information Governance Officer. An additional Insurance Officer post is vacant. The CCGM post has already failed one recruitment round and is being advertised a second time. The report explicitly states these departures will leave Information Governance, Insurance and Risk Management service areas without any staff cover.
findings.matters: The council's ability to manage compliance, risk and fraud detection will be severely impaired while these positions are unfilled, creating material control gaps that a lender would find unacceptable.
findings.figures: Four key staff leaving; one failed CCGM recruitment; one ongoing vacancy for Insurance Officer
findings.quote: These departures will leave the Information Governance, Insurance and Risk Management service areas without any staff cover. There has been one failed attempt to recruit to the CCGM post and at the time of writing it is currently being advertised for a second time... Failure to recruit to these posts will present a significant risk to the Council in terms of service delivery to customers, governance and risk management.

news_drafts.headline: Gross interest earned on investments fell to £545k from £607k despite investment balances quadrupling to £12.4m
news_drafts.lead: As investment rates compress, the same cash balance generates less income, reducing financial flexibility. This constrains the council's ability to fund activities from investment returns and may force reliance on other sources or spending discipline.
news_drafts.paper_title: Treasury Management & Prudential Indicators Annual Report 2025/26

news_drafts.headline: The £10m March 2026 borrowing was structured for 5 years because the council is forecasting PWLB longer-term rates to decline within that period
news_drafts.lead: If PWLB rates do not fall as forecast and the council must refinance in 5 years at higher rates, it will have foregone the opportunity to lock in current rates. This is a material interest-rate risk for both the lender and council.
news_drafts.paper_title: Treasury Management & Prudential Indicators Annual Report 2025/26

news_drafts.headline: HRA financing cost ratio deteriorated to 11.30% (actual) from 10.42% (budgeted), showing worsening debt burden relative to revenue
news_drafts.lead: Rising financing cost ratios signal increasing debt burden or shrinking revenue, both red flags for affordability. The HRA's ability to service its self-financing debt is directly tied to this ratio; deterioration limits flexibility and absorbs revenue…
news_drafts.paper_title: Treasury Management & Prudential Indicators Annual Report 2025/26
